## Why Does Quizzing Yourself Beat Rereading?


**Quizzing yourself beats rereading because each act of recall strengthens the memory you retrieve, an effect that researchers call the testing effect or retrieval practice.** Rereading feels productive because the page looks familiar. Familiarity is recognition, and an exam asks for recall. A practice quiz trains the skill the exam measures.


The cleanest demonstration is Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke's 2006 study in *Psychological Science* . In their second experiment, students learned short prose passages on one of three schedules. One group read the passage four times. One group read it three times and recalled it once. One group read it once and recalled it three times. Half the students took a final test after five minutes, and half took it after one week.


Schedule Recall after 5 minutes Recall after 1 week


Read 4 times (SSSS) 83% 40%


Read 3 times, recall once (SSST) 78% 56%


Read once, recall 3 times (STTT) 71% 61%


Source: Roediger and Karpicke (2006), *Psychological Science* 17(3), 249-255, Experiment 2.


Two results in that table explain most of this guide. First, the ranking flips. Rereading wins at five minutes and loses at one week, which is why cramming feels effective and fails on exam day. Second, the students who reread predicted that they would remember more. The method that felt best was the method that worked worst. A quiz corrects that false feeling with a score.


### Four more findings that shape how you use a practice quiz


The testing effect is not one lucky experiment. It holds across materials, ages and settings, and later studies sharpened how to use it:


- **Recall beats elaborate study, too.** Karpicke and Blunt (2011, *Science* ) found that retrieval practice beat concept mapping on a test one week later, on both verbatim and inference questions.
- **Keep testing what you already know.** Karpicke and Roediger (2008, *Science* ) found that dropping a word pair from testing after one correct recall sharply cut recall a week later. Dropping it from further study did not. A question you got right once is not done.
- **A failed attempt still helps.** Kornell, Hays and Bjork (2009) and Richland, Kornell and Kao (2009) found that an unsuccessful attempt to answer, followed by the correct answer, improved later learning. A pretest before you read is useful even when you score low.
- **The effect holds in real classrooms.** Agarwal, Nunes and Blunt (2021, *Educational Psychology Review* ) reviewed classroom experiments and found that retrieval practice consistently benefits student learning.


Meta-analyses agree. Rowland (2014, *Psychological Bulletin* ) and Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan (2017, *Review of Educational Research* ) each pooled many studies and found a reliable advantage for practice tests over restudy. Pan and Rickard (2018) found that the benefit also carries over to new questions, though less reliably than to repeated ones. That is why this guide asks for application questions, not only the same definition again.


### Where self-testing ranks among study methods


In 2013, John Dunlosky and four colleagues reviewed ten popular study techniques for *Psychological Science in the Public Interest* . They rated each by how well the evidence supports it across learners, materials and test types.


Study technique Utility rating (Dunlosky et al., 2013)


Practice testing High


Distributed practice (spacing) High


Interleaved practice Moderate


Elaborative interrogation ("why is this true?") Moderate


Self-explanation Moderate


Summarization Low


Highlighting and underlining Low


Keyword mnemonic Low


Imagery for text Low


Rereading Low


The two high-utility methods work best together: practice tests, spread out over time. An AI quiz generator removes the slowest part of the first method, which is writing the questions. Spacing is still your job, and the[spaced repetition guide](https://www.taskade.com/blog/spaced-repetition-explained) covers it in depth.


Two related ideas explain why effort is the point. The generation effect (Slamecka and Graf, 1978) shows that information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you read. Robert and Elizabeth Bjork's "desirable difficulties" (2011) describes conditions that slow learning in the moment, such as recall, generation and spacing, and build stronger long-term memory. A quiz that feels easy is often a quiz that teaches little.

## Why Is a Practice Quiz Metacognition in Practice?


**A practice quiz is metacognition in practice because it shows you what you do not know before the exam does.** Metacognition is the ability to monitor and control your own thinking. John Flavell named the field in 1979. Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens (1990) split it into monitoring, which asks "how well do I know this?", and control, which asks "what do I study next?"


Most learners monitor badly. Their sense of knowing comes from fluency: the page reads smoothly, so the material feels learned. Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell (2013, *Annual Review of Psychology* ) review a long list of these illusions. A survey by Karpicke, Butler and Roediger (2009, *Memory* ) found that most students listed rereading as a study strategy, and few listed self-testing as their first choice. The students who most need an outside check rarely use one.


A quiz replaces the feeling with a measurement. Steve Fleming, a cognitive neuroscientist who studies metacognition, measures it as the match between confidence and performance (Fleming, *Know Thyself* , 2021). You can run the same measurement on yourself with one habit: before you check each answer, rate your confidence.


The four combinations of confidence and result each tell you something different:


Your confidence Your answer What it means What to do next


High Correct You know it and you know that you know it Keep it in rotation at longer gaps


Low Correct You know it but do not trust it Review the explanation. Butler, Karpicke and Roediger (2008) found that feedback helps keep these answers


Low Wrong A known gap Restudy the source section, then retry


High Wrong A false belief, the most dangerous result Fix it at once. Butterfield and Metcalfe (2001) found that high-confidence errors are often corrected well after feedback


This is also why "grade the homework" is the most useful skill in the AI era. A tool can write the questions for you, but only you can decide which wrong answers matter. Our explainer on[what metacognition is](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-is-metacognition) goes deeper, and the[Feynman technique](https://www.taskade.com/blog/feynman-technique) is the same idea in a different form: explain the topic from memory and see where you stall.

## What Question Types Should an AI Quiz Generator Write?


**A good AI quiz generator writes a mix of question types, because each type tests a different level of knowing.** Multiple choice and true or false test recognition. Short answer and cloze questions test recall. Application, explain-why and worked problems test whether you can use the idea. A quiz made only of recognition questions overstates what you know.


Question type What it tests Recall or recognition Watch for


Multiple choice Picking the right option from 3 to 5 Recognition Weak distractors that give the answer away


True or false One claim at a time Recognition A 50% guess rate and trick wording


Short answer Producing a term, fact or reason Recall Answer keys that accept only one exact phrase


Cloze (fill in the blank) A key term inside a sentence from the source Recall Blanks on trivial words instead of key terms


Matching Pairs, such as term to definition Recognition Elimination: the last pair answers itself


Application or scenario Using a concept in a new case Recall plus transfer Scenarios that restate the textbook example


Explain why Reasons and mechanisms Recall plus explanation No model answer to compare against


Ordering or sequence Steps of a process or a timeline Recall Partial credit that the tool does not give


Worked problem Math, physics, accounting or code Procedure and recall Answer-only keys with no steps


The research on format is consistent. Kang, McDermott and Roediger (2007) found that when feedback followed, short-answer practice produced better final-test performance than multiple-choice practice. McDaniel and colleagues (2007) found the same pattern in a real online college course. But multiple choice is not useless. Little, Bjork, Bjork and Angello (2012, *Psychological Science* ) found that multiple-choice questions with plausible, competitive options made learners think about why each wrong option was wrong, and that improved later recall of related facts.


There is also a risk in multiple choice. Roediger and Marsh (2005) found that students sometimes learned a wrong option as a fact, and the effect grew with more options. Butler and Roediger (2008) found that feedback after the test reduced this effect. So read the explanation for every multiple-choice question, including the ones you got right.


The ladder above follows the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001). Most AI quiz generators write at the bottom two rungs by default. You get higher rungs when you ask for them by name.

## How Do You Judge an AI-Written Quiz?


**Judge an AI-written quiz on three questions: does it test recall or only recognition, are the wrong options plausible, and does it explain wrong answers with a pointer to your source?** A quiz that passes all three teaches. A quiz that fails them gives you a score that means little. Run the checklist below on the first five questions of any new tool before you trust the rest.


Check A pass looks like A fail looks like


1. Grounded in your source Each answer appears in your PDF, notes or video Facts that are not in your material


2. Correct answer key The marked answer is right on every item you check A wrong option marked as correct


3. Recall, not only recognition Short answer and cloze items in the mix Only multiple choice and true or false


4. Plausible distractors Wrong options a confused learner would pick Joke options, or options from another subject


5. One best answer Exactly one option is defensible Two options are both right


6. Important content Questions on key ideas and relationships Questions on page numbers, dates of minor events, names of examples


7. Clear stem The question makes sense without the options You must read the options to understand the question


8. No giveaways Options of similar length and grammar The longest, most precise option is always right


9. Explanations Why the right answer is right, and why each wrong option is wrong Only "Correct" or "Incorrect"


10. Source pointer A page, section or timestamp for each answer No way to find the answer in your material


11. Coverage Questions from every section you assigned Ten questions from the first two pages


12. Control You can set types, difficulty, count and focus One fixed format


### What makes a good distractor


A distractor is a wrong option in a multiple-choice question. Item-writing research is clear on what works. Haladyna, Downing and Rodriguez (2002) reviewed decades of guidance and recommend plausible distractors based on common errors, options of similar length, and no "all of the above". Rodriguez's 2005 meta-analysis of 80 years of research found that three options are usually enough: a fourth or fifth option is often so weak that no one picks it. Gierl and colleagues (2017, *Review of Educational Research* ) reviewed how to build and analyze distractors and stress that each one has to reflect a real misconception.


Distractor problem Example for "What does mitochondrial DNA pass through?" Why it fails


Absurd option "The cell wall of a bacterium" Nobody picks it, so it tests nothing


Off-topic option "The Krebs cycle" Belongs to a different question


Grammar clue Only one option fits the sentence The grammar gives the answer away


Length clue The right answer is twice as long and precise Test-wise learners guess it


Near-duplicate "The mother" and "The maternal line" Two right answers


Good distractor "The father" A real, common misconception

## 1. Gemini Notebook (Formerly NotebookLM): Best Free Quizzes From Your Own Sources


**[Gemini Notebook](https://notebook.google/) writes flashcards and quizzes only from the sources you add to a notebook, and explains the answers you get wrong.** Google announced the rename from NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook on its blog on July 16, 2026, and said it remains a standalone product. Many older guides still use the NotebookLM name, so search for both.


**How it quizzes you.** You add sources to a notebook: class notes, readings, lecture recordings and other materials. In the Studio panel you pick Quiz or Flashcards. Google's November 2025 announcement says that you can choose the subject, set the difficulty and pick how many questions you want. You can also select and unselect sources for one output, so a quiz can cover only this week's chapter. Google's student page says the quizzes come "with detailed explanations for incorrect answers."


**Strengths.**


- Grounding is the core design. Google says responses stay grounded in the information you provide, which reduces off-topic questions from the open web.
- Source selection gives fine control. You can quiz yourself on one lecture, then on the whole unit.
- The same notebook also makes study guides, audio overviews and mind maps, so one upload feeds several study methods.


**Limits.** Google's plans page lists a base plan "for personal projects" with up to 50 sources per notebook and standard limits. Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra raise the source cap to 100, 300 and up to 600 and raise usage limits. The page lists no prices. Quizzes live inside the notebook. We found no quiz export on Google's pages, so a long-term question bank needs a second tool. Google also says grounding reduces, not removes, the chance of AI errors, so check answer keys on hard topics.

## 2. Quizlet: Best for Practice Tests Beside a Large Study-Set Library


**[Quizlet](https://quizlet.com/) turns your notes, slides or readings into AI practice tests, and it sits beside one of the largest libraries of study sets on the web.** Its AI test generator page says you can upload a .docx, .pdf or .pptx file, connect your Drive, or paste text, and get multiple-choice and short-answer questions. That mix of recall and recognition is a good default for self-testing.


**How it quizzes you.** You create a practice test from your material, or you study an existing set in Quizlet's long-standing Learn and Test modes. Learn mode mixes question formats as you study. Test mode builds a scored test from a set. For many learners, the value is the network: a set for a standard textbook chapter often already exists, and you can test yourself on it before you write a single question.


**Strengths.**


- Practice tests take the three common file formats, Google Drive and pasted text, so most class material goes in without conversion.
- Short-answer questions in the practice test push you toward recall, not only recognition.
- Learn mode, Test mode and flashcards share one set, so you can move from drills to a full test on the same material.

We could not open Quizlet's help pages to confirm its status, so this guide does not rely on it. Public sets written by other learners vary in quality. ## 6. RemNote: Best for Explanations on Every Option


**[RemNote](https://www.remnote.com/) generates exam-style multiple-choice questions from a PDF or from your notes, with an explanation for both correct and incorrect answers.** Its AI quiz maker page says that "every question includes detailed AI explanations for both correct and incorrect answers." That is the feedback design the research supports for multiple choice, because it reduces the risk of learning a wrong option as a fact.


**How it quizzes you.** You upload a PDF or select text inside your RemNote notes. The tool writes multiple-choice questions. Its FAQ says every question is editable, you can customize structure and difficulty, and you can create conceptual or factual prompts. RemNote is a note-taking app first, so a quiz sits next to the notes it came from.


**Strengths.**

## How to Turn a PDF, Notes or a Video Into a Practice Quiz


**To turn your material into a useful practice quiz, give the AI a clean source, ask for a recall-heavy mix, answer from memory with a confidence rating, and bring missed questions back on a schedule.** The eight steps below work with any tool in this guide. The tool changes the buttons, not the method.


### Step 1: Prepare one clean source


Give the tool one chapter, one lecture or one study guide at a time. Smaller sources give more focused questions and make the answer key easier to check. For a PDF, confirm that the text is selectable. If it is a scan, use a tool that names scan or handwriting support. Our guides to[PDF to notes tools](https://www.taskade.com/blog/pdf-to-notes) and[YouTube to notes tools](https://www.taskade.com/blog/youtube-to-notes) cover how to prepare a clean source first.


### Step 2: Take a short pretest before you study


Generate five questions and answer them before you read. You will miss most of them. The pretesting research (Richland, Kornell and Kao, 2009) found that a failed attempt followed by the answer still improves later learning, and the questions tell you what to look for while you read.


### Step 3: Ask for a recall-heavy mix


Ask for the question types by name. A prompt that works in any chat-based tool:


```text
From the attached chapter only, write a 20-question practice quiz:
- 6 short-answer questions
- 4 fill-in-the-blank questions on key terms
- 5 multiple-choice questions with 3 plausible options each, based on common misconceptions
- 3 application questions that use a concept in a new case
- 2 "explain why" questions with a model answer


For every question, give the correct answer, a one-sentence explanation,
why each wrong option is wrong, and the page or section it comes from.
Do not ask about page numbers, figure numbers or the names of examples.
Put the answer key after all the questions.


```


### Step 4: Audit the answer key


Check every answer against the source before your first attempt. This takes a few minutes for 20 questions and protects you from memorizing an error. Run theten-minute audit the first time you use a new tool.


### Step 5: Answer from memory and rate your confidence


Close the source. Write or type each answer before you look at options or the key. Then mark your confidence as low, medium or high. This one habit turns a quiz into a metacognition check.


### Step 6: Read every explanation


Read the explanation for every question, including the ones you got right. Feedback is what limits the risk of learning a wrong option (Butler and Roediger, 2008). It also locks in correct answers you were unsure of.


### Step 7: Log what you missed


Keep a short list: the question, your wrong answer, your confidence, the topic and the source page. High-confidence misses go to the top. The log is your study plan for the next session.


### Step 8: Space the retests


Retake missed questions after a day, then after a few days, then after a week. Keep correct questions in the rotation at longer gaps. Thenext section gives a schedule.


Each question moves through a simple life cycle. A question leaves your rotation only after you answer it correctly after a delay, not after the first correct answer:


### For a PDF: the PDF to quiz workflow


A PDF to quiz converter works best on a text-based PDF of one chapter. Upload it, ask for questions from one section at a time, and check the key against the page. For a full course, a study guide is often a better source than the textbook, because it already lists what matters. Taskade's[PDF to quiz converters](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf-to-quiz) cover textbooks, study guides and manuals. A[PDF to study guide](https://www.taskade.com/convert/pdf/pdf-to-study-guide) step before the quiz can make the questions more focused.


### For a YouTube video: the YouTube to quiz workflow


Most YouTube to quiz tools read the video transcript or captions. A video with no captions gives weak questions or none. Ask for the timestamp of each answer, so that a missed question sends you back to the right minute of the lecture.


### For notes: the notes to quiz workflow


Your own notes make the most relevant quiz, because they hold what your instructor stressed. They also hold your mistakes. Before you trust a notes to quiz key, check key facts against the textbook or slides. Short notes give thin quizzes, so add the related reading as a second source when the tool allows it.

## How Often Should You Quiz Yourself Before an Exam?


**Quiz yourself in several short sessions spread over days or weeks, and keep correct questions in rotation, because spaced retrieval beats one long session.** Cepeda and colleagues' 2006 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin* found a strong benefit for spreading practice out. Their 2008 study in *Psychological Science* found that the best gap between sessions grows as the time to the test grows.


The schedule below is a practical plan for a four-week runway, based on those findings. It is our recommendation, not a published protocol:


Time before the exam Session Focus


4 weeks Pretest plus first quiz on units 1 and 2 Find gaps early


3 weeks New quiz on units 3 and 4, retest misses from units 1 and 2 Mix old and new


2 weeks Mixed quiz across all units Interleave topics


10 days Retest every missed and low-confidence question Close known gaps


1 week Full practice test in the exam format, timed Format match


3 days Retest misses from the practice test Fix false beliefs


1 day Short mixed quiz, then rest Confidence check, not cramming


Two more findings shape the schedule. First, mix topics within a session. Rohrer and Taylor (2007) found that shuffled practice problems produced better test performance than problems blocked by type, because the learner has to pick the method, as on an exam. Second, do not drop a question after one correct answer. Karpicke and Roediger (2008) showed that continued testing of known items mattered for recall a week later. For the full method, read our[spaced repetition explainer](https://www.taskade.com/blog/spaced-repetition-explained) . ## What Do AI Quiz Generators Get Wrong?


**AI quiz generators get answers wrong, ask about trivia, skip sections and overstate what you know when they write only recognition questions.** Every vendor in this guide that addresses accuracy says the same thing in its own words: check the output. That is not a reason to skip these tools. It is a reason to audit them.


Failure Why it happens What to do


A wrong answer marked as correct The model misreads the source or fills a gap from general knowledge Check the key against the source before your first attempt


A question your source does not support The model adds facts from outside your material Ask for "from the attached source only", and use grounded tools


Trivial questions Dates, names of examples and page details are easy to extract Ask for key ideas and relationships only


Coverage gaps Long sources get cut or the model focuses on early pages Generate per section, check a stated page limit


Recognition-only quizzes Multiple choice is the default output of many tools Ask for short answer, cloze and application by name


Weak distractors Plausible errors are harder to write than absurd ones Edit distractors into real misconceptions


Transcript and scan errors Captions and text recognition misread terms Fix the source text first, or check flagged terms


No memory of your misses Chat tools and one-off generators keep no bank Log misses yourself, or use a tool that keeps questions


Do not ask the same AI to grade its own key and accept the result. Huang and colleagues (2023, presented at ICLR 2024) found that large language models often fail to correct their own reasoning without outside feedback, and sometimes make it worse. Your source is the outside feedback. A short look at the page beats a second opinion from the same model.


Privacy is the other limit. You upload class notes, readings and sometimes personal material. Some vendors state a clear rule: Kahoot says it processes uploads transiently and does not use them to train models, Adobe says it deletes files unless you sign in to save them, and Google says that individual Gemini Notebook data is not used for training unless you share feedback. Read the rule for any tool before you upload material you would not share.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is the best AI quiz generator in 2026?


It depends on your source and your goal. Gemini Notebook, formerly NotebookLM, writes quizzes only from the sources you add. Quizgecko reads files, links and videos and lets you pick question types. Knowt has a free Learn mode, StudyFetch builds timed practice tests in the format of your exam, and Revisely assesses written answers. Taskade turns a PDF, notes or a video into an editable quiz and keeps your questions, explanations and review schedule in one workspace.


Can AI turn a PDF into a quiz?


Yes. Most AI quiz generators read a PDF and write multiple choice, true or false, short answer and fill-in-the-blank questions with an answer key. Check two limits first: how many pages the tool reads, and whether it can read a scanned PDF. Revisely's free plan reads 5 pages per document and its paid plans read 200, and Questgen reads PDFs up to 100 pages.


How do I make a quiz from a YouTube video?


Paste the video link into a YouTube to quiz tool. Most of these tools read the video transcript or captions, so a video with no captions gives weak questions or none. Ask for the timestamp of each answer, so that you can jump back to the part of the video you missed.


What is the best free AI quiz maker for students?


Gemini Notebook has a base plan for personal projects with up to 50 sources per notebook. Knowt's free Learn mode has no usage cap. Adobe's online quiz maker needs no sign-up. Quizgecko has a free plan, and Questgen gives 20 free runs. On Taskade Free, you earn free AI credits with referrals and invites, and you can upgrade any time.


Are AI-generated quizzes accurate?


Mostly, but not always. An AI quiz generator can mark a wrong option as correct, write a question your source does not support, or test a trivial detail. Check each answer against your source before you trust your score, and treat an explanation that does not cite the source as a claim to verify.


Is multiple choice or short answer better for studying?


Short answer usually builds stronger memory because you must recall the answer, not recognize it. Kang, McDermott and Roediger found in 2007 that short-answer practice with feedback beat multiple-choice practice on a later test. Multiple choice still helps when the wrong options are plausible and you read the feedback. Use both.


How often should I quiz myself before an exam?


Quiz yourself in several short sessions spread over days or weeks, not in one long session the night before. Spacing research by Cepeda and colleagues shows that the best gap between sessions grows with the time until the test. Keep a question in rotation even after you get it right once.


Does quizzing yourself really work better than rereading?


Yes. In Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, students who read a passage once and recalled it three times remembered 61 percent of it a week later. Students who read it four times remembered 40 percent, even though they felt more confident. Dunlosky and colleagues in 2013 rated practice testing as a high-utility study method.


Can ChatGPT make a practice test from my notes?


Yes. ChatGPT study mode can quiz you one question at a time and give feedback on your answers, and it is available across ChatGPT plans. OpenAI's help page asks you to verify important information, so check important answers. A general chatbot also keeps no question bank or score history unless you build one.


What is the difference between an AI quiz generator and a flashcard maker?


A flashcard maker writes one prompt and one answer per card for fast, repeated review of facts. An AI quiz generator writes mixed question types, including multiple choice, short answer and application questions, and scores a full attempt. Flashcards suit vocabulary and definitions. Quizzes show whether you can use the ideas.

Yes, but a teacher's needs differ from a learner's. Teachers need answer keys, exam versions, LMS export and grading. This guide covers self-testing.
